prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and of firm-level trade data.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged from round 1: B026, Melitz and Helpman, as a single prize part. My alternatives have changed. B007 replaces B001. The discovery is that gains from trade depend on selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. It has two attributes I weigh heavily as someone who works on replicability. The central claim is clear and testable, and it has been tested repeatedly. Two decades of firm-level data from many countries have confronted it: exporter premia, selection into exporting, and productivity effects of liberalisation. The welfare magnitudes are sensitive to functional form. The qualitative selection and reallocation result has nonetheless held up across datasets and settings, and I count that as the kind of durability a prize should reward. Attribution is comparatively tractable. Melitz (2003) is the originating model. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his broader heterogeneous-firm agenda, make him the natural second name. I take the chair's question on distinctness from the 2008 prize seriously. I read the 2008 prize as covering scale economies, intra-industry trade and location with representative firms. Selection across firms is a different channel, tested on micro data that did not exist then. The exchange has not moved my ranking of B026 first. It has made me more explicit about what the citation must claim. It should honour the heterogeneous-firm framework and not all firm-level trade research.
statement.case_against: The main weakness is attribution at the edges. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made parallel empirical and quantitative contributions, and none of them is credited on this ballot entry. A Melitz-Helpman prize could look like under-crediting the empirical establishment of exporter facts. The heterogeneous-firm framework also sits close to the 2008 trade prize, and I can argue distinctness but cannot prove it. Some welfare conclusions depend on assumptions such as the productivity distribution. B012 has a broader policy footprint, and B007 has a cleaner two-author attribution. On those two dimensions my preferred part is weaker. I do not claim that cleaner attribution is more important than breadth of influence. I weigh both, and I rank B026 first mainly because of the repeated empirical testing of its central claim.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B007 first and B026 second. He agrees that Melitz (2003) is the anchor and that Redding is an extension. He says the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line is not credited on this ballot entry, so the Committee would have to explain why Helpman is the second name. He prefers B007 because its two-author credit has no obvious missing claimant.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection to my configuration, and I do not think it can be fully answered. The parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum model is a real contribution, and the empirical exporter-premium facts it connects to preceded the theory. Two considerations still lead me to keep Helpman. First, the Committee here can credit only the names on the entry, so the choice is between Helpman and no second name, and Helpman's Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI is a distinct extension of the framework to firm organisation. Second, the citation can be worded around the theoretical framework of heterogeneity and selection, so that it does not imply that the empirical and quantitative strands are unrecognised. I agree that B007 has cleaner attribution. I treat that as a point about credit, not as proof that B007 is the larger discovery.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only, after dropping Gertler. He calls B026 a close alternative and says a Melitz-Helpman pair is not clean until the Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum questions and Helpman's credit across trade lines are settled. He would prefer B026 on breadth of influence if the Committee finds Melitz's originating role sufficient.
responses.response: I accept the narrowing to two names, and it improves the B007 case. The exchange moved B007 into my alternatives, above B001. My difference from Krusell now rests on evidence, and I would not call it a difference in importance. The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is clear and shaped post-2008 thinking, but several colleagues agree that collateral channels are identified less cleanly than the theory. That includes Boppart, Strömberg and Krusell. The selection and reallocation result in trade has been confronted with micro data more directly. On Helpman's credit across trade lines, I do not think it weakens his claim here. His Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work stands on its own. I would still want the Committee to say explicitly why the pair is not premature, and I think the Melitz-originated framework answers that.

responses.point: Strömberg proposes a two-part prize: Kiyotaki and Moore (B007) and Melitz alone (B026). He acknowledges that the one-person B026 part may look like a product of the three-laureate cap. He says he would support Melitz and Helpman together if B026 stood alone.
responses.response: I appreciate that he supports Melitz and Helpman together if B026 stands alone, and I agree that Melitz-only is a worse attribution because it drops the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work. I do not support the combined configuration. The two achievements are unrelated: one is a macro-finance mechanism and the other a trade framework. Joining them mainly gathers support from two groups, and I do not take that as evidence of merit. The cap also forces the Melitz-only part, which he himself says looks like an artefact. If the Committee wants a two-part prize, I would rather keep Helpman and shorten the credit on B007 than drop Helpman. My preference is still a single part. I would regard his configuration as defensible on merit, but weaker on attribution than either part standing alone.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and now lists B026 as an alternative. He accepts that firm heterogeneity is distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize. He remains concerned that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are not credited and that Helpman also appears under a trade-politics entry, so B026 is less clean than it looks. He also shares my concern about the robustness of B001.
responses.response: I agree that B026 is less clean than the two-name proposal suggests, and the Bernard-Jensen-Eaton-Kortum question is the strongest point against it. On Helpman appearing under another entry, I think that shows his breadth and does not weaken the heterogeneous-firm claim. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple stands as a separate piece of work. I keep B012 as my first alternative. If the Committee chooses it, I would treat Calvo and Woodford as the core, which agrees with his own remark that the Taylor rule is the thinnest element. Friberg's point is also relevant to my views. Micro price data pointing to state-dependent adjustment qualifies Calvo's time-dependent mechanism. It concerns refinement more than origination, but it leaves me less certain about B012 than about B026.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would regard the omission of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum as serious enough to make a Melitz-Helpman pair premature. Whether Helpman is the right second name beside Melitz is also open.
Whether selection and reallocation across firms is distinct enough from the 2008 prize. I think it is, but I cannot settle that from the written record alone.
Whether Redding should be added for the quantitative and spatial extensions, or whether that is a separate discovery.
How much to weigh B012's breadth of policy influence against its diffuse credit, the micro evidence on state-dependent pricing, and the unresolved post-2021 record.
Whether the empirical identification concerns about collateral channels in B007 are permanent weaknesses or the normal state of a mature theoretical mechanism.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or the empirical record beyond the supplied evidence and my own reading.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz or Helpman, or to any credited name in the alternatives B012 and B007. My listed frequent co-authors, including Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johannesson and Rand, are not credited on the shortlist. I note two things I do not treat as conflicts. I have SSE ties to Ellingsen and Johannesson, who are former committee members. My field of metascience and replicability shapes how heavily I weigh repeated empirical testing, and I disclose that as a perspective and not as a candidate tie.
